mainTopic: מעילה with קונמות, how much one must eat to break an oath, and a new משנה on oaths about eating and drinking
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא about whether מעילה applies to things forbidden by a קונם. The גמרא reverses the opinions so that רבי מאיר says there is no מעילה with קונמות. It then explains that his statement 'קונמות כשבועות' was only an argument made according to the view of חכמים. חכמים answer that the reasoning of רב פנחס applies to שבועות but not to קונמות. Next רבא rules that eating dirt does not break a general oath not to eat. He then asks how much dirt or grape seed breaks an oath that names them, and both questions end in תיקו. רב אשי asks the same question about a נזיר and a grape seed. It is answered from ריש לקיש's words: a plain oath on an already-forbidden food means a כזית. The proof does not carry over to dirt, because dirt is not food at all. A new משנה then teaches how many קרבנות a person owes for breaking oaths about eating and drinking, and how inedible and forbidden foods are treated. The גמרא opens with שמואל's rule that drinking breaks an oath not to eat, supported both by logic and by a פסוק.

steps.title: חכמים say there is no מעילה with a קונם
steps.stepSummary: The last line of the ברייתא gives the view of חכמים: no one commits מעילה by eating something forbidden by a קונם, because מעילה does not apply to קונמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And חכמים say: neither the person himself nor his friend commits מעילה, because there is no מעילה with קונמות.
steps.whatsHappening: We are hearing the end of a ברייתא that the גמרא is already in the middle of quoting. Here חכמים say that eating a food forbidden by a קונם is never מעילה, no matter who eats it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קונם is a vow that makes an object forbidden 'like הקדש'. The question is whether that also brings the penalty of מעילה, the special sin of using holy property. חכמים here say no. The earlier part of the ברייתא (before this line) gave רבי מאיר's view that the vower himself does commit מעילה.

keyTerms.meaning: Misusing הקדש (holy) property for personal benefit; brings a קרבן and a payment
He committed מעילה
Plural of קוּנָּם: vows that make an item forbidden as if it were הקדש
His fellow, the other person

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין הוּא וּבֵין חֲבֵירוֹ לֹא מָעַל,
phrases.english: both he and his fellow did not commit misuse,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the one who made the קונם on himself; 'his fellow' is someone else who ate the item.

phrases.english: because there is no misuse with konamot.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: בֵּין הוּא וּבֵין חֲבֵירוֹ לֹא מָעַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a ברייתא that the גמרא began quoting before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to חכמים in the ברייתא as first quoted, there is no מעילה at all with קונמות.

steps.title: Reverse the opinions in the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא swaps the two views. רבי מאיר says no one commits מעילה with a קונם. חכמים say the vower does commit מעילה, but his friend does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Reverse it: neither this one nor that one commits מעילה, because there is no מעילה with קונמות. These are the words of רבי מאיר. And חכמים say: he commits מעילה, and his friend does not.
steps.whatsHappening: To fix a problem raised before this section, the גמרא says to switch who said what in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the views are swapped, the strict view (the vower commits מעילה) belongs to חכמים. The lenient view (no מעילה at all with קונמות) belongs to רבי מאיר. This fixes the earlier difficulty, but it will create a new one in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Reverse, meaning switch the opinions between the speakers
Both this one and that one

steps.confusionAlert: After the reversal, 'there is no מעילה with קונמות' is now רבי מאיר's view, not the view of חכמים. Keep this switch in mind for the rest of the discussion.

phrases.english: Reverse it:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה לֹא מָעַל,
phrases.english: both this one and that one did not commit misuse,
because there is no misuse with konamot.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Rabbis say:
he committed misuse, and his fellow did not commit misuse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rewrites the ברייתא quoted in step 1 by swapping its speakers.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא as written gives רבי מאיר the view that the vower commits מעילה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Read the ברייתא reversed: רבי מאיר says there is no מעילה with קונמות, and חכמים say the vower commits מעילה.

steps.title: How can רבי מאיר compare קונמות to שבועות?
steps.stepSummary: If רבי מאיר holds there is no מעילה at all with קונמות, why did he say 'קונמות כשבועות'? That statement only says they don't add up together, which suggests מעילה does apply to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, how does רבי מאיר say 'קונמות are like שבועות'? That means only that קונמות do not combine, but מעילה does apply to them! But רבי מאיר said there is no מעילה with קונמות at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reversal from step 2. It points to another statement of רבי מאיר that seems to assume מעילה does apply to a קונם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'קונמות כשבועות' means that small amounts of different קונם items do not add up to the minimum for מעילה. If adding up is the only thing that is missing, then מעילה must apply in principle. But after the reversal, רבי מאיר says there is no מעילה at all. So the two statements seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Like oaths
Combining, adding small amounts together to reach a minimum
But didn't he say?! (introduces a contradiction)
At all

phrases.english: If so,
Rabbi Meir says konamot are like oaths –

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא קוּנָּמוֹת אִצְטְרוֹפֵי הוּא דְּלָא מִצְטָרְפִי,
phrases.english: so it is only that konamot do not combine,
but misuse does apply to them?!
But didn't Rabbi Meir say:
there is no misuse with konamot at all!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר קוּנָּמוֹת כִּשְׁבוּעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reversal made in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reversed version of the ברייתא, which has רבי מאיר saying there is no מעילה with קונמות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'קונמות כשבועות' takes away only the adding-up, which implies מעילה applies. That clashes with saying there is no מעילה at all.

steps.title: רבי מאיר was arguing by חכמים's own view
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר said 'קונמות כשבועות' only according to the view of חכמים. His own view is that there is no מעילה at all, but he asks them to agree at least that קונמות are like שבועות.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was speaking to חכמים according to their own view: 'In my view, there is no מעילה with קונמות at all. In your view, at least agree with me that קונמות are like שבועות!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question in step 3. 'קונמות כשבועות' was not רבי מאיר's own position. It was a point he made using the view of חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר holds there is no מעילה with a קונם at all. Since חכמים disagree and say מעילה does apply, he tells them that even by their view, a קונם should work like a שבועה, so small amounts don't add up. That way there is no contradiction, and the reversal from step 2 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: According to their words, arguing from the other side's view
According to me, in my view
According to you, in your view
At least agree with me

steps.whatToRemember: After the reversal, רבי מאיר holds there is no מעילה with קונמות at all. His statement 'קונמות כשבועות' is only a fallback argument he makes according to the view of חכמים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a common move in the גמרא: a תנא says something 'לדבריהם' (by the other side's view) that is not his own opinion. You need to know this to avoid seeing contradictions where there are none.

phrases.english: He is speaking to them according to the words of the Rabbis:
According to me – there is no misuse with konamot at all;
according to you – at least admit to me
that konamot are like oaths!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Speaking according to the other side's view (לדבריהם)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'קונמות כשבועות' is רבי מאיר's own view, so he must hold that מעילה applies to a קונם.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר holds there is no מעילה at all. He says 'קונמות כשבועות' only as an argument by the view of חכמים.

steps.title: Why חכמים treat שבועות and קונמות differently
steps.stepSummary: חכמים hold that the reasoning of רב פנחס applies to שבועות, so they don't add up together. It does not apply to קונמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how do חכמים explain it? With שבועות, the reasoning of רב פנחס applies. With קונמות, the reasoning of רב פנחס does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how חכמים can say that שבועות don't add up together while קונמות are different: the reasoning of רב פנחס applies only to oaths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 4, רבי מאיר asked חכמים to agree that קונמות are 'like שבועות'. Here the גמרא gives חכמים' answer: they don't accept that comparison. The reason oaths don't add up (רב פנחס's reasoning) just doesn't fit קונמות.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis, the same as חכמים
There is / there is not (it applies / it does not apply)

steps.whatToRemember: חכמים: oaths don't add up because of רב פנחס's reasoning, but that reasoning doesn't carry over to קונמות. So the comparison 'קונמות כשבועות' is רבי מאיר's request, not חכמים' view.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
phrases.notes: This is a short question: how do חכמים explain why they don't accept that קונמות are like שבועות?

phrases.english: With oaths, the reasoning of רב פנחס applies;
with konamot, the reasoning of רב פנחס does not apply.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the side of חכמים after Step 4 explained רבי מאיר's request that they agree קונמות are like שבועות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the reasoning: the reason that applies to oaths does not apply to konamot
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think חכמים must agree that קונמות and שבועות work the same way.
steps.terutzMaskana: חכמים separate them: רב פנחס's reasoning applies only to שבועות.

steps.title: An oath not to eat does not cover eating dirt
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if someone swore 'I will not eat' and then ate dirt, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If someone said, 'On my oath, I will not eat,' and then ate dirt, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבא rules that eating dirt does not break a general oath not to eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A general oath 'I will not eat' only covers real food, the kinds of things people eat. Dirt is not food, so eating it is not 'eating' under the oath. This ruling sets up the questions that follow.

keyTerms.meaning: 'On my oath, I will not eat'
Dirt, earth
Exempt, not liable

phrases.english: Rava said:
If one said, 'On my oath, I will not eat,'
and he ate dirt, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, separate from the קונמות discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general oath not to eat does not include dirt, since dirt is not food.

steps.title: How much dirt breaks an oath not to eat dirt
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks: if someone swore specifically not to eat dirt, does he need to eat a כזית, or any amount at all? The question stays unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: If someone said, 'On my oath, I will not eat dirt,' how much must he eat? Since he said 'I will not eat,' maybe he means a כזית, the normal amount for eating. Or maybe, since dirt is not something people eat, he means any amount at all? The question stands unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks how much dirt a person must eat to break an oath that names dirt specifically. The גמרא leaves it as תיקו, unresolved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One side: the word 'eat' normally means a כזית, so that is what he meant. Other side: nobody eats a כזית of dirt, so he probably meant even a tiny bit. Both sides make sense, so there is no answer.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (a real question with two possible sides)
How much? (what amount makes him liable)
An olive-size amount, the normal measure for eating
Any amount, even a tiny bit
'Let it stand': the question is left unresolved

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the same case as Step 6. There he swore 'I will not eat' in general, and dirt was not included. Here he named dirt directly, so dirt is surely included. The only question is how much.

phrases.english: Rava asked:
If one said, 'On my oath, I will not eat dirt,' how much must he eat to be liable?
Since he said 'I will not eat,'
his intention is for an olive-size amount;
or perhaps, since it is not something
that people eat,
he is liable for any amount?
Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 6: dirt isn't included in a general oath, but what if he names dirt directly?
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does an oath not to eat dirt mean a כזית or any amount?

steps.title: How much grape seed breaks an oath not to eat grape seeds
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks the same kind of question about a grape seed, which people eat only mixed in with the grape. It also stays unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: If someone said, 'On my oath, I will not eat a grape seed,' how much must he eat? Since it does get eaten as part of a mixture, maybe he means a כזית. Or maybe, since people don't eat it by itself, he means any amount? The question stands unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks a second question about an oath on grape seeds. Again the גמרא leaves it as תיקו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A grape seed is in-between: unlike dirt, people do eat it, but only inside the grape. One side says that makes it real food, so a כזית is needed. The other side says that since nobody eats seeds on their own, he meant even a tiny bit.

keyTerms.meaning: Grape seed
Through a mixture (eaten together with the grape)
By itself, in its own form
Any tiny amount

phrases.english: Rava asked:
If one said, 'On my oath, I will not eat a grape seed,' how much must he eat to be liable?
Since it is eaten as part of a mixture,
his intention is for an olive-size amount;
or perhaps, since not by itself
do people eat it,
his intention is for any tiny amount?
Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel question to Step 7, now about something that is eaten, but only in a mixture.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does an oath not to eat a grape seed mean a כזית or any amount?

steps.title: A נזיר who swears not to eat a grape seed
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks: a נזיר is already forbidden by the Torah to eat a כזית of grape seeds. If he swears not to eat them, does his oath cover any amount, or still only a כזית?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי asked: If a נזיר said, 'On my oath, I will not eat a grape seed,' how much must he eat? Since a כזית is already forbidden to him by the Torah, maybe his oath is about what is still permitted, so he means any tiny amount. Or maybe, since he said 'I will not eat,' he means a כזית?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי asks a new version of the grape-seed question, this time about a נזיר. The גמרא tries to answer it starting in the next step, and the proof is accepted in Step 14.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath can't take hold on something the Torah already forbids, so for a נזיר a כזית of grape seeds is already covered. One side: he must have meant the permitted part, a tiny amount, so his oath has something to do. Other side: 'I will not eat' always means a כזית, whatever the result.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who took a vow to be a nazirite and may not eat grape products
A Torah prohibition
Something permitted
He swears, takes an oath

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a key idea: a person's oath is read by what he would sensibly mean. If the plain meaning would make his oath pointless, maybe he meant something else.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi asked:

phrases.aramaic: נָזִיר שֶׁאָמַר ״שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל חַרְצָן״, בְּכַמָּה?
phrases.english: A nazirite who said, 'On my oath, I will not eat a grape seed,' how much must he eat to be liable?
phrases.notes: A נזיר may not eat grape seeds (במדבר 6:4).

phrases.english: Since an olive-size amount is already a Torah prohibition,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי קָא מִשְׁתְּבַע – אַהֶתֵּירָא קָא מִשְׁתְּבַע,
phrases.english: when he swears, he is swearing about what is permitted,
phrases.notes: What is still permitted to a נזיר is less than a כזית, so that is what his oath would be about.

phrases.english: and his intention is for any tiny amount;
or perhaps, since he said 'I will not eat,'
his intention is for an olive-size amount?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes רבא's grape-seed question from Step 8 and applies it to a נזיר, for whom a כזית is already forbidden.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: When a נזיר swears not to eat a grape seed, does the oath cover any amount (the permitted part) or a כזית?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Answered in Step 14: from ריש לקיש's statement, a plain oath on an already-forbidden food means a כזית, so the נזיר is liable only for a כזית.

steps.title: Bringing a משנה about swearing not to eat and then eating non-kosher food
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens an attempted proof for רב אשי's question by quoting a משנה. Someone who swore not to eat and then ate נבילות, טריפות, שקצים or רמשים is liable. רבי שמעון exempts him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'An oath that I will not eat,' and then he ate carcasses, טריפות, repugnant creatures and creeping animals: he is liable. רבי שמעון exempts him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a proof for רב אשי's question by quoting a משנה. The actual proof will only come a few steps later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case in the משנה is like the נזיר case: the food is already forbidden by the Torah, and then a person adds an oath on top. The משנה says the oath still makes him liable. That gives the גמרא a starting point for the question of how much he must eat.

keyTerms.meaning: Meat of animals that died without proper שחיטה
Animals with a fatal defect, forbidden to eat
Repugnant creatures and creeping animals, all non-kosher

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"An oath that I will not eat,"
and he ate carcasses and tereifot,
repugnant creatures and creeping animals – he is liable.
And Rabbi Shimon exempts him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to resolve רב אשי's question from Step 9
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's question: does an oath on an already-forbidden food mean any amount or a כזית?
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about swearing not to eat and then eating נבילות and טריפות

steps.title: How can the oath work on food that is already forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls its own earlier question on that משנה. Why is he liable for breaking his oath? He is already sworn from הר סיני not to eat these foods.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we discussed it: Why is he liable? He is already sworn from הר סיני!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting its own earlier challenge on the משנה. An oath should not be able to take effect on food the Torah already forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that a new oath cannot take hold of something that is already forbidden by the Torah. So it seems the oath should mean nothing for non-kosher food. The answers to this challenge in the next steps are what the proof will rest on.

keyTerms.meaning: And we discussed it: quoting an earlier discussion
Already sworn from Sinai: the Torah already forbids it

phrases.english: And we discussed it:
Why is he liable?
He is already sworn from Mount Sinai!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of the משנה just quoted
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that he is liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An oath cannot take effect on something already forbidden by the Torah

steps.title: רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן: he also included permitted foods
steps.stepSummary: רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן answer that the oath also included permitted foods. Because it takes hold on those, it covers the forbidden foods too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן say: It is a case where he included permitted things together with forbidden things.
steps.whatsHappening: Three אמוראים answer the challenge. The oath worked because it also covered permitted foods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath that includes permitted items does take hold. Once it takes hold on those, it can stretch to cover the forbidden items in the same oath. This answer is quoted only to complete the picture; the proof will come from ריש לקיש's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Including: one oath that covers several items together
Permitted things
Forbidden things

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan, who say:
It is where he includes permitted things
together with forbidden things.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the oath also included permitted foods
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The oath seemed to be only on forbidden food, so it could not take effect
steps.terutzMaskana: The oath included permitted foods, so it took hold on everything

steps.title: ריש לקיש: specifying a half-measure, or following רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says there are only two ways to explain it. Either he specified a חצי שיעור, following the חכמים. Or he swore with no amount specified, following רבי עקיבא, who says an oath covers any amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: You can only find this case in one of two ways. Either he specified a half-measure, according to the חכמים. Or he swore without specifying, according to רבי עקיבא, who says a person can forbid himself even the smallest amount.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives a different answer. The oath works only because it covers an amount smaller than what the Torah forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah only punishes eating a כזית of forbidden food. Below a כזית there is no Torah penalty, so an oath can take hold there. According to the חכמים he must say this out loud ('even a half-measure'). According to רבי עקיבא, any oath automatically means even the smallest amount.

keyTerms.meaning: Specifies: says the detail out loud in the oath
Half-measure: less than the normal amount (a כזית)
Unspecified: a plain oath with no amount mentioned
Any amount at all, even tiny

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two views. For the חכמים, a plain oath means a כזית, and only 'I said even a half-measure' covers less. For רבי עקיבא, every oath covers any amount automatically.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish said:
You cannot find it except
either where he specifies a half-measure,
and according to the Rabbis;
or with an unspecified oath,
and according to Rabbi Akiva, who says:
a person can forbid himself with any amount at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר: אִי אַתָּה מוֹצֵא אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the challenge of Step 11, different from Step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: the oath covers an amount smaller than the Torah's prohibition
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The oath was on food the Torah already forbids, so it could not take effect
steps.terutzMaskana: The oath took hold on less than a כזית, either by specifying (חכמים) or automatically (רבי עקיבא)

steps.title: Proof: with nothing specified, the oath means a כזית
steps.stepSummary: נבילה is already forbidden from הר סיני, just like a grape seed for a נזיר. ריש לקיש needed the person to specify a half-measure according to the חכמים. So without specifying, he means a כזית, and this answers רב אשי's question.
steps.simpleTranslation: But נבילה is something he is already sworn about from הר סיני, just like a grape seed for a נזיר. The only reason he is liable for less is that he specified it. If he did not specify, he meant a כזית. Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now makes its proof from ריש לקיש's words. A plain oath on an already-forbidden food covers only a כזית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case of נבילה matches רב אשי's case exactly: a food the Torah already forbids, with an oath added on top. According to the חכמים, ריש לקיש needed the person to specify a half-measure. That shows a plain oath on such a food means a כזית, so the נזיר's oath also means a כזית.

keyTerms.meaning: Grape seed, forbidden to a נזיר
His intention is for an olive-sized amount
Learn from it: the proof is accepted

phrases.english: But a carcass –
it is something he is already sworn about from Mount Sinai,
so it is just like a grape seed for a nazir;
and the reason he is liable is that he specified,
but if he did not specify –
his intention is for a kezayis!
Learn from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא נְבֵילָה דְּמוּשְׁבָּע וְעוֹמֵד מֵהַר סִינַי הוּא

steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's statement that, according to the חכמים, he must specify a half-measure

steps.title: Then רבא's question about dirt should be solved too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. If it works, it should also solve רבא's question about an oath on dirt, since נבילה is like dirt. Without specifying, the answer would be a כזית. But רבא's question was left unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then you should also solve what רבא asked: 'An oath that I will not eat dirt' — how much must he eat? Solve it: not until there is a כזית, since נבילה is like dirt. The only reason he is liable for less is that he specified; if he did not specify, he meant a כזית!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges its own proof. The same reasoning would also solve רבא's question about dirt, which was treated as unresolved. The answer to this challenge comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נבילה is not normal food for this person, just like dirt. So if the proof is good for the grape seed, it is equally good for dirt. Since רבא's question about dirt stayed open (Step 7), the proof must have a weakness somewhere.

keyTerms.meaning: Resolve: settle the open question
Dirt
How much: what amount makes him liable

phrases.english: But then resolve what Rava asked:
phrases.notes: This is רבא's open question from earlier, about swearing not to eat dirt.

Resolve that he is not liable until there is a kezayis –
for a carcass is like dirt;

but if he did not specify – his intention is for a kezayis!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof of Step 14 by showing it proves too much
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof in Step 14 from ריש לקיש's statement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same reasoning would solve רבא's dirt question, which was left unresolved, so the proof must be flawed

steps.title: Dirt is not food, but a carcass is
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the challenge from Step 15. Dirt is not food at all, while נבילה is real food that is only blocked by an איסור. So the proof about נבילה cannot settle רבא's question about dirt.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Dirt is not food at all. A carcass is food, but a lion is crouching on top of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on Step 15 and explains why נבילה and dirt are not the same. That keeps the proof for רב אשי's question standing, while רבא's question about dirt stays unresolved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 claimed that נבילה is just like dirt, so a proof about one should solve the other. This step shows the difference: נבילה is real food, and only the Torah's איסור stops a person from eating it. Dirt is not food in any way, so how much a person means when he swears about dirt is a separate question.

keyTerms.meaning: dirt, earth
something that is edible, fit to be eaten
a lion crouching over it, a picture for an איסור that blocks a food that is otherwise edible

steps.whatToRemember: נבילה is real food with an איסור on it. Dirt is not food at all. That difference is why the proof works for רב אשי's question but not for רבא's.

phrases.english: No.

phrases.aramaic: עָפָר – לָאו בַּר אֲכִילָה הוּא כְּלָל;
phrases.english: Dirt is not edible at all;
a carcass is edible,
but a lion is crouching over it.
phrases.notes: The "lion" is the Torah's איסור. The meat itself is food, but the איסור stands guard and keeps you away from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא; עָפָר – לָאו בַּר אֲכִילָה הוּא כְּלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends the proof in Step 14 by rejecting the comparison to dirt made in Step 15.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that נבילה and dirt are the same for this question.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Dirt is not food at all, while נבילה is food blocked only by an איסור. The two cases are not the same.

steps.title: How many offerings for breaking an oath about eating and drinking
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה teaches the counting rule. If he made a general oath, he owes only one קרבן, no matter how many things he ate or drank. If he named each item separately, he owes a separate קרבן for each one.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says "I swear I will not eat" and then eats and drinks, he owes only one. If he says "I swear I will not eat and I will not drink" and does both, he owes two. If he says "I swear I will not eat" and eats wheat, barley and spelt bread, he owes one. If he names all three breads in his oath, he owes one for each. The same pattern applies to drinking: a general oath means one, and naming wine, oil and honey means one for each.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches that the number of קרבנות a person owes depends on how many separate things he named in his oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A general oath like "I will not eat" is one oath, so breaking it in many ways still costs only one קרבן. Even drinking is covered by a plain oath not to eat, since he owes only one for eating and drinking together. When he names each item separately, each name counts as its own oath, so each one brings its own liability.

keyTerms.meaning: the משנה
an oath that I will not eat
liable for one, meaning one קרבן
spelt, a kind of grain
for each and every one

steps.confusionAlert: The number of קרבנות does not depend on how many foods he ate. It depends on how many items he named in his oath.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
"An oath that I will not eat,"
and he ate and drank:

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל וְאָכַל וְשָׁתָה

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general oath brings one קרבן no matter how many items he ate or drank. Naming each item separately brings a separate קרבן for each.

steps.title: Inedible foods and forbidden foods under an oath
steps.stepSummary: If he swore not to eat and then ate something that is not fit to eat, he is exempt. If he ate foods the Torah forbids, such as נבילות, he is liable, but רבי שמעון exempts him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he swore "I will not eat" and then ate foods that are not fit to eat or drank liquids that are not fit to drink, he is exempt. If he swore "I will not eat" and ate נבילות, טריפות, שקצים or רמשים, he is liable. רבי שמעון says he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with two cases: eating things that are not really food, and eating real food that the Torah already forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating something inedible is not considered eating, so it does not break the oath. Forbidden foods are real food, so the חכמים hold him liable. רבי שמעון exempts him, which ties back to the earlier question of an oath that tries to take hold on something already forbidden from הר סיני.

keyTerms.meaning: foods that are not fit to be eaten
meat of animals that were not slaughtered properly, and animals with a fatal defect
non-kosher creatures and creeping animals
exempt

phrases.english: "An oath that I will not eat,"
and he ate foods that are not fit for eating,

phrases.aramaic: וְשָׁתָה מַשְׁקִין שֶׁאֵינָן רְאוּיִן לִשְׁתִיָּה – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: or drank liquids that are not fit for drinking: he is exempt.
"An oath that I will not eat,"

phrases.aramaic: וְאָכַל נְבֵילוֹת וּטְרֵיפוֹת, שְׁקָצִים וּרְמָשִׂים – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: and he ate carcasses and טריפות, repugnant creatures and creeping animals: he is liable.
And Rabbi Shimon exempts him.
phrases.notes: He is already sworn from הר סיני not to eat these, as the גמרא discussed back in Step 11.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל וְאָכַל אֳוכָלִין שֶׁאֵינָן רְאוּיִן לַאֲכִילָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה with cases of inedible foods and forbidden foods.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating inedible food does not break the oath. Eating forbidden food does break it according to the חכמים, while רבי שמעון exempts him.

steps.title: A קונם on his wife that depends on whether he ate
steps.stepSummary: If he declared a קונם that his wife may not benefit from him if he ate today, and he had eaten forbidden foods, his wife becomes forbidden to benefit from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said, "My wife is forbidden to benefit from me as a קונם if I ate today," and he had eaten נבילות, טריפות, שקצים or רמשים, his wife is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends with a different kind of case. Here a קונם depends on whether he ate, and the question is whether eating forbidden food counts as eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case nobody needs a new oath to take hold on forbidden food. The only question is whether he "ate," and he truly did. So even רבי שמעון would agree that his wife is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: a type of נדר that forbids something as if it were a קרבן
benefits from me
forbidden

steps.whatToRemember: Forbidden foods still count as "eating." The only debate is whether a new oath can take hold on them.

phrases.english: If he said: "קונם that my wife benefits from me
if I ate today,"

phrases.aramaic: וְהוּא אָכַל נְבֵילוֹת וּטְרֵיפוֹת, שְׁקָצִים וּרְמָשִׂים –
phrases.english: and he had eaten carcasses and טריפות, repugnant creatures and creeping animals:
his wife is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קוּנָּם אִשְׁתִּי נֶהֱנֵית לִי אִם אָכַלְתִּי הַיּוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a final case to the משנה that shows forbidden food still counts as eating.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A קונם that depends on whether he ate takes effect even if what he ate was forbidden food.

steps.title: שמואל: drinking breaks an oath not to eat
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבין quotes שמואל. Someone who swore not to eat is liable if he drinks. The גמרא then says this can be supported by logic or by a פסוק, which sets up the next steps.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבין said in the name of שמואל: if he swore "I will not eat" and then drank, he is liable. You can support this with logic if you want, or with a פסוק if you want.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה with שמואל's ruling that drinking counts as eating for an oath. It then announces two possible sources, setting up the explanations that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said that one who ate and drank owes only one קרבן, but it did not say whether drinking alone breaks the oath. שמואל adds that it does: drinking alone is enough to make him liable. The line "either logic or a פסוק" is a setup, and the גמרא will now give both.

keyTerms.meaning: the גמרא
if you want, say
a logical argument
a פסוק

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the plain words "I will not eat" also cover drinking, which explains the first ruling of the משנה.

phrases.english: GEMARA:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin said that Shmuel said:
"An oath that I will not eat," and he drank: he is liable.
If you want, say a logical argument;
and if you want, say a verse.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא on the new משנה by expanding its first ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath not to eat is broken by drinking, and he is liable.

steps.title: Proof from logic: everyday speech counts drinking as eating
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports שמואל's rule with a logical argument from how people talk. When someone says 'let's taste something,' the friends end up eating and drinking.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, you can prove it from logic. A person says to his friend, 'Let's taste something,' and then they go in and both eat and drink.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its first support for שמואל's rule that a שבועה not to eat also forbids drinking. The support is simple logic based on how people normally speak.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שבועה follows the way people normally use words. Since ordinary speech treats an invitation to 'taste' or eat as including drinks, a person who swore not to eat also meant not to drink. So drinking breaks his שבועה.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say. This introduces one of two possible ways to prove something.
Logic, a reasoned argument rather than a פסוק
Let's taste something, an everyday invitation to a snack or a meal
They drink

phrases.english: If you wish, say a logical argument:
For a person says to his friend:
"Let's taste something,"
and they go in and eat and drink.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fulfills the first half of the promise in Step 20 that שמואל's rule can be supported by logic or by a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's rule that one who swore not to eat is liable if he drinks
steps.raayaSupportSource: Everyday speech: an invitation to 'taste something' leads to both eating and drinking

steps.title: Proof from a פסוק: ריש לקיש shows drinking is included in eating
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a second support from the Torah. ריש לקיש brings a פסוק about מעשר שני that says 'you shall eat' and then lists תירוש, which is wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, you can prove it from a פסוק: drinking is included in eating. As ריש לקיש said: How do we know that drinking is included in eating? Because it says: 'And you shall eat before ה׳ your God, in the place He will choose to rest His name there, the tithe of your grain and your wine.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its second support for שמואל's rule, this time from a פסוק. It quotes ריש לקיש, who shows from the Torah that drinking counts as eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses the word 'eat' (וְאָכַלְתָּ) and then lists תירוש, which is wine, as one of the things to be 'eaten.' Since wine is drunk, the Torah's own wording treats drinking as part of eating. That backs up the idea that a שבועה not to eat also covers drinking.

keyTerms.meaning: A פסוק, a Torah verse used as a source
Drinking is included in eating
Tithe. Here it means מעשר שני, which is eaten in ירושלים
New wine, a drink

steps.whatToRemember: Two supports for שמואל's rule: logic (people say 'let's taste' and then eat and drink) and a פסוק (the Torah says 'eat' about wine). Either way, drinking falls under eating.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think ריש לקיש is saying drinking and eating are the same in every case. He is only showing that the word 'eating' can include drinking.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say a verse:
drinking is included in eating;

For it is said: "And you shall eat before ה׳ your God,

the tithe of your grain and of your wine";
phrases.notes: דברים 14:23. Watch the word תירוש: it means wine, a drink, yet the פסוק says 'eat.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, independent support (a פסוק) alongside the logical argument of Step 21.
steps.raayaObject: That drinking is included in eating, which supports שמואל's rule
